title: Tzav: first, the ashes (Leviticus 6:3–4)
hook: each day the priest begins by clearing yesterday's ashes, in plain clothes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the altar fire that must never go out. Your line was keep the fire. Did you add your one small log? Day three hundred eighty-six.

What's the first job of your morning? The phone, the coffee, last night's dishes staring back. In the sanctuary, as the rabbis describe the day, the first job wasn't a grand prayer or a beautiful offering. It was cleaning. Before anything new could happen on the altar, someone had to deal with what was left from yesterday. The fire had burned all night. There were ashes. And the Torah gives that humble job careful instructions, right down to what the priest should wear.
screen: `THE FIRST JOB OF THE DAY.` → `NOT A PRAYER. CLEANING.` → `RIGHT DOWN TO THE CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the verses describe. The priest puts on his linen priestly garments. He lifts a portion of the ashes from the altar and sets it beside the altar. Then he takes off those garments and puts on other ones, and carries the rest of the ashes out of the camp, to a clean place. The rabbis called this terumat ha-deshen, the lifting of the ashes, and it was the first act of the Temple day. Notice the two changes of clothes. The first part, lifting the ashes at the altar, is done in full priestly linen. This dirty job counts as holy service. But for hauling the ashes out, the priest changes into plainer clothes. Rashi explains with a picture from a household: the clothes a servant wears to cook a pot for his master aren't the clothes he wears to pour his master's wine. Each job gets the right clothes, and both are service. Then the Mishnah adds a story. In the Temple, it says, this job was so sought after that priests would race up the ramp of the altar to win the right to do it. Whoever got within four cubits first won the job. Once, two were racing neck and neck, one pushed the other, and he fell and broke his leg. After that, the court decided it by lottery. Grown men, competing to be the one who cleans up. The day's holiness began with yesterday's ashes, cleared first, and cleared gladly.
screen: `TERUMAT HA-DESHEN: LIFTING THE ASHES.` · `LINEN AT THE ALTAR, PLAIN CLOTHES OUTSIDE.` · `THE RACE UP THE RAMP.` · `DECIDED BY LOTTERY.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE ASHES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear yesterday's ashes. Settle, and breathe. Look around you, or picture the space where you'll be today: your desk, your kitchen, your car, your inbox. What's left over from yesterday? Dirty cups, unread messages, a pile on a chair. Pick one small patch. Then picture clearing it, carefully, as the first act of your day, not a chore to resent but the job that makes room for what's new. And if there's inner ash too, an old irritation, notice it, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
Tzav. Command. The portion where every day in the sanctuary begins by clearing yesterday's ashes.
Your line: clear the ashes first. Tomorrow morning, before anything new, clear one small thing left from the day before. Day three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: The lifting of the ashes, terumat ha-deshen, is described in the Mishnah's tractates Tamid and Yoma, and some prayer books include its passages among the morning readings about the Temple service.

original.note: Hebrew: the lifting of the ashes, the first service of the Temple day.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone had to clean up the altar.
what it means: the first holy act of every day was clearing yesterday's ashes, in priestly linen.

what a scholar hears: Mishnah Yoma 2:1–2 tells of the race up the ramp and the lottery that replaced it; Rashi on 6:4 compares the garment change to a servant's clothes for cooking versus pouring wine.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they do first in the morning, and no longer says the Torah set the ashes as the day's first job (that order is the Mishnah's); cut the stock 'the part people remember'.
Leviticus 6:3–4 paraphrased (numbering per JPS; 6:10–11 in Christian Bibles).
The outline's 'in plain clothes' applies to carrying the ashes out (6:4); the lifting itself is done in linen priestly garments (6:3). The script reflects both.
Rashi on 6:4 (cooking clothes vs. wine-pouring clothes): confirm.
Mishnah Yoma 2:1–2: race up the ramp, within four cubits; the broken-leg incident and the lottery: confirm details.
